Tidal locking, a phenomenon where a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, profoundly shapes planetary climates across the universe. This gravitational handshake between a planet and its star creates worlds of dramatic extremes, challenging our understanding of habitability.

The most striking consequence is the permanent division between a scorched dayside and a frozen nightside. On tidally locked exoplanets orbiting red dwarf stars, the dayside endures eternal daylight, potentially heating surfaces beyond 1,000°C on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero. This temperature gradient drives one of the most fascinating climate features: supersonic winds. Air heated on the dayside rises and rushes toward the nightside, creating atmospheric circulation patterns unlike anything in our solar system.

Atmospheres play a decisive role in determining whether these worlds remain habitable. A thick atmosphere can redistribute heat effectively, moderating the temperature extremes and potentially keeping water liquid across a wider region. The terminator zone—the twilight band between day and night—may harbor the most hospitable conditions, where temperatures could allow liquid water and stable climates. Some scientists propose this "terminator habitability" could make these twilight zones prime candidates in the search for life.

However, tidal locking also poses serious threats to habitability. Dayside conditions may be hot enough to vaporize water, which then becomes permanently trapped as ice on the nightside—a process called atmospheric collapse or "eye of the eye" effect... wait,
